newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico hopes to solve land problem by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Mexico hopes to solve land problem by 2000.

text.p: Mexico's countryside has been languishing in poverty for three decades but changes in land laws should allow investors to step in and revitalise the rural economy, a government minister said on Wednesday.
Agrarian Reform minister Arturo Warman told foreign correspondents the government hoped to arrange proper land titles for almost all of Mexico's 27,200 communal farms, or ejidos, by 2000.

This would give the farms a more secure future, encourage them to invest more in improving their land and help attract fresh investment from outside to raise productivity and combat dire poverty, he added.

"Mexico cannot be an advanced, democratic country with such a big, impoverished countryside," Warman said. Hauling peasants out of poverty was "an essential part of the democratic modernisation of Mexico", he added.
The ejidos, born out of the peasants' cry for land during the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, control over half of Mexico's land but much of it is arid, sterile terrain unsuitable for cultivation.
With an average of 130 members each, ejidos typically use primitive farming methods including horse-drawn carts. Most lack the capital to buy machinery or to improve techniques.
Warman said that since the 1960s, Mexico's agricultural growth had lagged well behind other sectors such as industry and services and had barely kept pace with population growth.
Although a third of Mexicans eke out their living directly or indirectly from agriculture, the sector accounts for just 7-8 percent of the economy, Warman said.

But he said a landmark change in the law in 1992 giving ejidos ownership of their land -- it was previously considered state property -- and allowing them to divide up their communal land privately should help matters.

So far only around 250 ejidos, almost all located near towns where demand for building land was growing, had decided to dissolve their associations but there was a trend towards more private investment in the communal land, he added.
